title: Four-dimensional X-ray nano-holotomography reveals multiscale chemomechanics in composite graphite–silicon battery electrodes - Nature Nanotechnology
byline: Vanpeene; Victor; Stamati; Olga; Cadiou; Francois; Jacquet; Quentin; Villanova; Julie; Lyonnard; Sandrine
html:
Abstract

Linking electrode microstructure to electrochemical performance is essential for optimizing Li-ion batteries. However, this requires mechanistic four-dimensional observations at the ultimate spatiotemporal scales, which remain elusive. Here we demonstrate the use of interrupted-operando synchrotron X-ray nano-holotomography combined with digital volume correlation to track chemomechanical dynamics at both particle (local) and electrode (averaged) scales. Quantitative scale-bridging image analysis is applied to composite graphite–silicon electrodes during their electrochemical formation cycle. Our findings reveal that local ionic diffusion properties, graphite particle morphology and position in the electrode, distance to silicon clusters, surface contact with the liquid electrolyte solution, and mechanical deformations all directly affect local electrochemical activity and irreversibility, although these parameters are not equally important. In particular, we identify fast ionic diffusion channels that play a key role and counterbalance intrinsic depth-dependent reaction heterogeneities arising from ionic and electronic diffusion limitations. The various structural factors that determine the electrochemical performance of composite graphite–silicon electrodes in Li-ion batteries beyond ensemble properties are classified using a scale of influence, providing a practical framework for the optimization of materials and electrode manufacturing.

Main

Li-ion battery electrode degradation involves complex, intertwined phenomena1. Although these mechanisms depend heavily on electrode microstructure and material properties, precisely controlling electrode architecture remains difficult. Empirical tuning of averaged parameters (particle size distribution and porosity) often fails to capture the three-dimensional (3D) multiscale complexity that governs electrochemical performance2,3,4. Understanding the intricate chemomechanical interactions that regulate electrode activity is therefore crucial for establishing structure–performance relationships beyond trial-and-error methods5.

Analysing the coupling between morphology and transport requires advanced methodologies to simultaneously monitor electrode dynamics at both particle and electrode scales. This presents experimental challenges: (1) resolving multiscale heterogeneities, (2) detecting poorly contrasting phases and (3) capturing dynamic microstructural evolution during battery cycling. Hence, 3D space-resolved approaches with tunable resolution are needed to determine the electrode hierarchical structure6,7 under representative operando conditions8. While various techniques exist, each typically addresses only one of these challenges. Particle-scale techniques such as scanning transmission electron microscopy coupled with electron energy loss spectroscopy (STEM–EELS)9,10, optical microscopy11,12,13, scanning transmission X-ray microscopy14,15 and diffraction-based techniques16,17,18,19 have provided valuable insights into lithiation mechanisms but lack electrode-level insight. Macroscopic techniques such as dilatometry20 and acoustic sensing21 capture global behaviour but miss local heterogeneity. Alternatively, synchrotron X-ray computed tomography (CT) offers advantages as a non-invasive 3D technique, capable of analysing various chemistries with excellent spatiotemporal resolution6,22,23,24,25,26,27. Combined with digital volume correlation (DVC)28,29, tomographic datasets can quantify 3D strain fields and mechanical failure modes in electrode materials such as graphite30 and graphite–silicon (Gr–Si) electrodes31. However, these electrode-level studies generally lack the submicrometre resolution necessary for comprehensive particle-scale analysis. X-ray nano-CT overcomes this limitation by combining large fields of view with high spatial resolution (≤200 nm)6. The propagation-based phase-contrast approach32,33 enables segmentation of low-attenuating materials, making it particularly valuable for light-element electrodes such as Gr–Si composites34,35. So far, nano-CT has been extensively used for post-mortem characterization36,37,38, but recent advances at fourth-generation synchrotrons have achieved acquisition times below tens of minutes at submicrometre resolution, enabling four-dimensional (3D + time) operando measurements during cell operation, provided that specialized battery cells, experimental set-ups and workflows are developed to ensure representativeness and reproducibility between measurements25.

Here, we demonstrate a methodology for multiscale interrupted-operando nano-CT measurements combined with DVC, applied to composite Gr–Si electrodes during formation cycling in Li metal cell configuration. Gr–Si material is ideal for probing chemomechanical coupling because silicon undergoes 300% volume expansion during lithiation39,40 and exhibits sequential (de)lithiation behaviour relative to graphite13,41. By analysing individual particles, particle subgroups and electrode-averaged features, we quantify and bridge local and ensemble micromechanical states unravelling the structure–performance relationship in Gr–Si electrodes.

Four-dimensional multiscale X-ray nano-imaging of the Gr–Si composite electrode

X-ray nano-imaging was performed using a dedicated multiscale set-up on a calendered industry-grade manufactured composite electrode consisting of graphite and nanosilicon (74 wt% and 11 wt%, respectively) mixed with binder and additives in a nano-CT custom lithium metal cell with no lithium limitation (Fig. 1a,b). Sample preparation, cell configuration and operando imaging set-up were optimized and standardized to reach the small sample size required for both high-resolution (pixel size of 50 nm) and high-contrast imaging, under representative conditions25 (Methods; Supplementary Figs. 1 and 2). The electrode is constituted of porous graphite particles (average diameter 12 µm) and silicon nanoparticles (nominal size 200 nm) that tend to form large aggregates (5–15 µm) of carbon-binder-domains–silicon (CBD–Si) randomly distributed throughout the electrode (Fig. 1b,c and Supplementary Figs. 2 and 3). The corresponding volume fraction (indicated as %v) underestimates the silicon content of the composite electrode (4.1%v versus 18%v in theory). Therefore, a substantial portion (75%) of the silicon material is intimately mixed with graphite particles or grafted onto their surfaces (Supplementary Figs. 2 and 3), remaining unresolved within the nano-CT volume, due to the limited spatial resolution (≤150 nm). Consequently, quantitative analysis of the silicon (de)lithiation mechanism is indirectly monitored by investigating its impact on graphite, through a detailed particle-by-particle morphological analysis.

a, Sketch of the operando nano-CT set-up at the ID16B beamline of ESRF featuring the electrochemical cell housed in a dedicated holder and connected to a potensiostat. b, Three-dimensional rendered images of the analysed Li metal cell assembly (Li|electrolyte solution-filled separator|Gr–Si composite electrode) imaged at 257 nm voxel size (orange corresponds to Cu current collectors, blue to the electrolyte-filled separator, and white with black stripes to the Gr–Si electrode) and zoom-in rendering at high magnification (50 nm voxel size) focused on the electrode and particle scale. c, Nano-CT reconstructed grey-scale slices acquired in operando conditions at different magnifications (257 and 50 nm voxel size) with a close-up view of one large CBD–Si cluster in 2D and 3D. d, The first formation cycle of the composite electrode in Li metal cell (applied current is 5.15 µA) with cell potential and capacity evolution (lithiation and delithiation of the working Gr–Si electrode) over time, along with the hourly acquisition steps indicated by the orange rectangles. e, Three-dimensional renderings of the reconstructed images of the Gr–Si electrode (50 nm voxel size) at specific time steps (initial state before cell cycling, end of first lithiation and end of first delithiation).

Electro-chemo-mechanical processes of the Gr–Si composite electrode were unravelled during its formation cycle in Li metal cells through interrupted-operando X-ray nano-CT within minutes of temporal resolution (Fig. 1d). In fact, holotomography scans consisted of four distances acquisition (total acquisition time of 9 min) and were acquired every hour during (de)lithiation steps performed at constant specific current (110 mA g−1) during which the cell relaxed to open circuit potential (OCP). The expected electrode swelling and contraction can be visually demonstrated (60 to 75 µm, and back to 64 µm), as shown in Fig. 1e. Note that particular attention was paid to limit the radiation dose received by the sample during the full experiment25,42 (≤1.5 MGy; Supplementary Note 3). This precaution ensures reliable electrochemical and 3D nano-imaging monitoring, further enabling quantitative investigation of the underlying dynamic mechanisms within the electrode down to the particle scale.

Morphological evolution of the composite Gr–Si electrode microstructure

The graphite particles and the electrode porosity have been isolated across the electrode using machine learning segmentation (Fig. 2a and Supplementary Note 4).

The global porosity network can be further divided into two main components: the interparticle porosity, associated with the electrode microstructure, and the intraparticle porosity (for example, inner-particle pores), characteristic of the active materials (Fig. 2a). Initially, at the OCP, they respectively account for 23%v and 12%v, hence 35%v for the global macroporosity in agreement with electrode specifications after calendering (30–35%). Relative changes in both the graphite and porosity volume fractions indicate a multistep sequential (de)lithiation process (Fig. 2b,c and Supplementary Video 1), where distinguishing inter- and intraporosities (shown as dark- and light-blue-coloured areas in the electrode total porosity curves of Fig. 2b,c) provides valuable information about the nature and function of the pore network beyond a simple global behaviour, enabled by the high spatial resolution of nano-CT.

During the initial lithiation of the composite Gr–Si working electrode, the graphite fraction and porosity remain balanced at cell potentials ≥60 mV, resulting in overall swelling of the electrode microstructure. Both inter- and intraparticle porosities follow the macroporosity trend (continuous line), with 40% contribution from inner pores. When the cell potentials are below 35 mV, the electrochemical system reaches the silicon activity domain, and a sudden porosity decrease is measured, extending from −7.5% to −17% (Fig. 2b, dashed line). At that stage, the inner pores contribution is only 20% (Fig. 2c and Supplementary Fig. 8a). During the subsequent delithiation, the porosity of the composite electrode progressively increases, with a larger step from −10% to −2.5% after reaching the cell potential of 175 mV (Fig. 2c, dashed line). This observation is consistent with a sequential process, with graphite delithiation followed by that of silicon41,43. The intraparticle porosity progressively increases through delithiation, eventually exceeding OCP levels (+18%; Supplementary Fig. 8a), indicating expansion of graphite intersheet spaces (average intrapore size of 420 nm versus 280 nm initially; Supplementary Fig. 8b) and formation of new pores in the carbon active material, observable as graphite sheet exfoliation (Fig. 2a, white arrows). The inner pore contribution is now up to 50% (Fig. 2c). This important contribution is usually not seen by micro-CT techniques owing to the lack of spatial resolution. These formerly inner surfaces, now exposed to the electrolyte solution, are prone to additional solid-electrolyte interface (SEI) formation during subsequent cycles, resulting in cumulative Li inventory loss. In addition, an interparticle porosity reduction of −15% is detected (Supplementary Fig. 8a,b), which could be associated with incomplete graphite delithiation and/or pore clogging induced by silicon electrochemical activity41,44,45.

Meanwhile, progressive and partially reversible grey-value changes towards lower (darker) values were observed within the CBD–Si clusters during cell cycling, compared with the electrolyte solution-filled separator regions used as reference (Fig. 2d,e, Supplementary Fig. 9 and Supplementary Note 4). To monitor these changes, the evolution of the corresponding grey-value integrated peak area within the examined clusters (representative of a quarter of the active silicon particles) was tracked during the initial cell formation cycle, serving as a metric for indirectly monitoring Si volume change during (de)lithiation. The results reveal a 120% increase in volume upon lithiation of the composite working electrode, with an irreversible swelling of +30% remaining after formation. This relative shift could result from enhanced SEI formation in these regions and/or incomplete delithiation of silicon particles. Note that a precise quantitative analysis of SEI/binder phases is beyond the scope of the present study. In addition, the grey-value evolution profile highlights distinct potential steps for silicon (de)lithiation, further supporting previous observations made at the electrode scale based on graphite particle analysis16. The kinetics and transition of the graphite lithiation staging process relative to silicon activity show that Si primarily reacts when stage 2/2L is pure (that is, for a Li metal cell discharge capacity of 600 mAh g−1), and to a lesser extent when graphite is fully lithiated (that is, for a Li metal cell discharge capacity of 800 mAh g−1), as monitored through operando wide-angle X-ray scattering (WAXS) mapping (Supplementary Fig. 5), in agreement with both our nano-CT data and previous scattering-based works46.

Chemomechanical evolution at the Gr–Si composite electrode scale

Detailed quantitative analysis of electrode microstructural deformation was performed using DVC, where subvolumes of 4 × 4 × 4 µm3 were locally tracked during the initial cell formation cycle, allowing measurement of 3D displacements and derived strain fields at the nanoscale. Displacement maps indicate the electrode expands and contracts as a whole from its centre of mass towards the separator and current collector sides during lithiation and delithiation, respectively (Fig. 3a and Supplementary Video 2). The mean values of measured orthogonal strain amplitudes indicate highly anisotropic electrode deformation, dominated by the through-thickness component (ϵzz = 8.8%; Fig. 3b), consistent with previous reports31,43. An asymmetric behaviour in magnitude is observed for in-plane deformation (ϵxx = 1.24%, ϵyy = 2.43%), highlighting microstructural rearrangements large enough to disrupt ionic diffusion pathways. Notably, the ϵyy component exhibits large irreversibility, a trend also reflected by volumetric and deviatoric strains (Fig. 3c).

summary: Particle-resolved 4D nano-tomography identifies fast ionic transport pathways as key regulators of electrochemical activity and reversibility in graphite–silicon battery electrodes.
